title: NASA JSC, Sony, Space Force, and Kingstown Capital
body:
## The Founding Engineers

When Stephen Altemus left the Johnson Space Center in 2013 to co-found Intuitive Machines, he carried with him something rarer than a government pension: institutional credibility earned in the worst circumstances American aerospace has known. On the morning of February 1, 2003, the Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry, killing all seven crew members. Altemus, then a senior engineer at JSC, was named Columbia Reconstruction Director — the person responsible for coordinating the physical and technical reconstruction of what the accident investigation board needed to understand the failure. It was among the most disciplined aerospace engineering management assignments in modern spaceflight history, a role demanding forensic rigor, interagency coordination, and the kind of institutional credibility that cannot be conferred by rank alone.

That credential preceded a tenure as JSC's Director of Engineering and eventually Deputy Director, the second-highest operational role at the centre that manages human spaceflight from mission control. Altemus, 62, holds a B.S. in Aeronautical Engineering from Embry Riddle Aeronautical University and an M.S. in Engineering Management from the University of Central Florida. He joined NASA in 1989 at Kennedy Space Center on the Space Shuttle Program. By the time he departed to co-found Intuitive Machines, he had spent twenty-four years inside the institutional infrastructure of American human spaceflight.

His co-founder brought a different kind of pedigree. Dr. Kamal Ghaffarian, 67, is the chairman of Intuitive Machines and one of the most prolific deep-tech founder-chairman figures of his generation. His academic formation — two undergraduate degrees, a master's in information management, and two doctorates in management information systems and technology — is the unusual product of someone who understood early that the bureaucratic and technical dimensions of aerospace contracting were inseparable. He built Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies from a services contractor into a firm substantial enough to attract KBR's acquisition in 2018. Since then, his portfolio of founder-chairman positions has expanded to include Axiom Space, the private orbital module operator; X Energy, the advanced nuclear reactor developer; Quantum Space, the cislunar intelligence startup; and PTX, among others. His chairmanship of Intuitive Machines is the institutional anchor that positions a co-founded startup to operate alongside companies with decades of government contracting history.

## A Board Configured for This Moment

The six-director board Altemus and Ghaffarian assembled is unusually calibrated for the specific phase of the business. As of May 2026, Intuitive Machines was executing the integration of its $800 million Lanteris Space Systems acquisition, managing a $4.82 billion NASA CLPS contract ceiling, and guiding a revenue ramp from the $250–300 million FY2025 range toward a $900 million–$1 billion FY2026 outlook. The board composition — national security, aerospace finance, corporate governance, and financial engineering — maps directly onto those four execution risks.

William J. Liquori, 57, is the Class I director providing the national security anchor. A retired Lieutenant General in the U.S. Space Force, Liquori served as Chief Strategy and Resourcing Officer — the officer responsible for budget architecture and long-range planning across the newest military branch. His B.A. in Computer Science from Boston University was followed by three graduate degrees: an M.S. in Computer Resources and Information Management from Webster University, and advanced military education at Air University (Airpower Art and Science) and Marine Corps University (Strategic Studies). He chairs the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee and the Conflicts Committee, and holds board seats at True Anomaly, the space situational awareness venture, and the Space Force Association. In the context of a company whose addressable market includes Space Force and Department of Defense infrastructure on and near the Moon, Liquori's institutional relationships are not incidental to the directorship — they are the point of it.

Robert L. Masson, 57, occupies the audit and aerospace finance seat. A 1992 Naval Academy graduate in economics who subsequently earned an MBA from Harvard Business School, Masson flew as a Naval Aviator until 2001 before transitioning to a career as a chief financial officer in defense and industrial manufacturing — Raytheon Technologies, Flowserve, Hypertherm, and Latham Group. He chairs the Audit Committee and sits on the Compensation, Nominating and Corporate Governance, Conflicts, and Strategic Transactions committees. He also chairs the audit committee at Tech-Etch, a precision-components manufacturer with defense applications. The Naval Academy + Harvard MBA + Raytheon + Naval Aviator pedigree is the precise credential profile for an audit committee chair overseeing NASA fixed-price contract accounting and the financial complexity of absorbing a satellite-systems business.

## The Financial Engineer and the Governance Architect

Michael Blitzer, 48, is the Class II director who is simultaneously the financial memory of LUNR's capital structure and its most active dealmaker. Blitzer founded Kingstown Capital Management in 2006, building it into a multi-billion-dollar asset manager serving endowments and foundations, before transitioning to chair Inflection Point Asset Management in 2024. The prior Inflection Point Acquisition Corp SPAC was the vehicle that took Intuitive Machines public via de-SPAC in February 2023. Blitzer holds a B.S. from Cornell and an MBA from Columbia Business School, where he also spent five years as an investing instructor. His institutional formation included Gotham Asset Management, the Joel Greenblatt-founded value fund, and an early career at J.P. Morgan Securities advising on private debt and capital raises.

By May 2026, his concurrent board roles made him the highest-frequency public-company capital-markets dealmaker on the board: Chairman of USA Rare Earth (Nasdaq: USAR) since its 2025 listing; Lead Independent Director at Merlin Labs (Nasdaq: MRLN); and active SPAC sponsorship through Inflection Point Acquisition Corps III and V. At Intuitive Machines, he chairs the Compensation Committee and the Strategic Transactions Committee — the body that approved the $800 million Lanteris acquisition. No director on the board was better positioned to evaluate whether that transaction's structure served shareholder interests.

Nicole Seligman, 69, rounds out the Class II directors and represents the most credentialed corporate-governance appointment on any U.S. listed company at LUNR's market capitalisation. She graduated magna cum laude from Harvard College and magna cum laude from Harvard Law School, clerked for Justice Thurgood Marshall at the U.S. Supreme Court, practised as a litigation partner at Williams & Connolly, and then spent a decade inside Sony Corporation, rising from Executive Vice President and Global General Counsel (2005–2014) to President of Sony Corporation of America (2012–2016) and President of Sony Entertainment (2014–2016). The Sony tenure involved managing legal, regulatory, and reputational risk for a Japanese conglomerate navigating U.S. regulatory frameworks across media, technology, and consumer electronics — experience that translates directly into the cross-jurisdictional complexity of a NASA-prime space systems company.

Her subsequent board appointments are the signal. She serves on the board of OpenAI — one of the small group of directors providing fiduciary oversight at arguably the most consequential technology company of the current decade. She also sits on the board of Meira GTx Holdings and Praetorian Acquisition Corp. At Intuitive Machines, she sits on the Audit, Nominating and Corporate Governance, and Conflicts committees. The Seligman appointment in June 2023 — four months after the de-SPAC listing — was a deliberate governance upgrade, signalling to institutional investors that the board understood the fiduciary obligations of a public NASA contractor.

## The Operators

Below the board, the executive team was substantially rebuilt around the Lanteris acquisition. Dr. Timothy Crain, 53, co-founded Intuitive Machines alongside Altemus and Ghaffarian and has served as Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer since February 2026. His PhD in Aerospace Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin preceded a NASA career at JSC that included navigation work on the Mars Science Lander and guidance, navigation, and control development for the Orion spacecraft. Crain is the engineering continuity of the company — the person whose institutional knowledge of the IM lander architecture extends back to the earliest design decisions of the program.

Peter McGrath, 58, joined as Chief Financial Officer in September 2024, arriving from a 31-year career at Boeing that covered structural analysis, Phantom Works advanced development, and launch services. He holds a B.S. and M.S. in Aerospace Engineering alongside an MBA. McGrath's background is precisely the profile that NASA's fixed-price CLPS contracting structure requires on the financial side: someone who understands the engineering economics of aerospace hardware well enough to model cost-to-complete with credibility.

Anna Jones, 47, became Senior Vice President, Chief Legal Officer, and Corporate Secretary in February 2026, the same month Crain's CTO appointment took effect. A J.D. graduate of Northwestern University School of Law, she had previously served as VP Securities and Corporate Counsel at Paysafe and held legal roles at Marathon Oil, ConocoPhillips, and Latham & Watkins. Her appointment as the company's first standalone CLO — rather than relying on outside counsel at the board-secretary level — reflected the legal complexity of managing a $4.82 billion NASA contract ceiling, an $800 million M&A integration, and the ongoing SEC reporting obligations of a post-de-SPAC listed company.

Chris Johnson, 49, is perhaps the acquisition's most tangible human asset. As the former CEO of Lanteris Space Systems and, before that, President of Boeing Satellite Systems International, Johnson brought the institutional manufacturing and systems-engineering capability that Intuitive Machines was buying when it agreed to pay $800 million for Lanteris. He earned a B.S. in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Kansas, an M.S. in Systems Architecting and Engineering from USC, and an MBA from USC, before spending more than two decades at Boeing in defence and commercial satellite roles. His appointment as President of Lanteris Space Systems in January 2026 — immediately upon the acquisition's close — placed him in operational control of the subsidiary that was expected to account for the majority of the revenue jump from the $250–300 million FY2025 range to the $900 million–$1 billion FY2026 outlook.

## The Architecture of the Bench

Taken together, the ten-person governance and executive structure Intuitive Machines assembled by May 2026 was configured for a specific inflection: the moment a lunar-logistics specialist becomes a space systems prime. Altemus and Crain carried the NASA engineering pedigree. Ghaffarian provided the institutional relationships and the founder's tolerance for the time horizons that deep-tech infrastructure requires. Liquori mapped the board to Pentagon and Space Force procurement relationships. Masson brought the aerospace-finance discipline to oversee NASA contract accounting. Blitzer provided the capital-markets architecture and the memory of the original public transaction. Seligman brought the governance credibility — and the OpenAI board seat — that institutional investors scrutinise when deciding whether a small-cap space company is ready for sustained ownership.

What the board notably lacked was a peer-CEO from the operating space industry — no equivalent of Tory Bruno or a sitting large-cap aerospace chief executive. That gap was deliberate: the board's job through the Lanteris integration and early CLPS task-order execution was governance and oversight, not operational second-guessing. The operators — Crain, McGrath, Jones, and Johnson — had been specifically recruited to execute. The board had been assembled to make sure the execution stayed within the bounds of what shareholders, NASA, and the Space Force would collectively tolerate.
